newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa needs fx controls - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa needs fx controls - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
Reacting to nagging yapping from the market, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has set out once more the prerequisites for a "big bang" removal of exchange controls.
Together with the minister of finance he has reaffirmed the gradualist approach to the removal of controls which, of course, are limited to residents.
The three conditions outlined by Stals that have to be in place are:
* the availability of foreign credit lines of about 15 billion rand, which could include a credit of $2 billion from the IMF linked to the current account deficit;
* a package of reconstruction measures, that would ensure a minimal outflow of foreign exchange;
* a political acceptance of the consequences of lifting exchange controls, principally the pressure on interest rates.

Now none of this is new. Even the 15 billion rand figure suggests he was reading from dated notes as that figure has been floated for many years and has not been updated for the depreciation of the rand. As far as we know such a line of credit has been in place a long time and continues to be so. It was heavily utilised in 1993, but was completely repaid by the end of 1995. It has been resorted to twice this year with a repayment being made in the following month.

The essence of this line of credit is its short-term nature and its use to maintain the requisite level of foreign exchange liquidity for the country. It is doubtful that it would be used to throw at the foreign exchange market to prop up the currency.

We seem to have forgotten that the country had already borrowed from the IMF to the amount of 2.8 billion rand in 1993. This too assisted in supporting foreign reserve position and not in supporting the currency. Any further borrowing from the IMF would only be granted on the grounds of a weakness in the current account.

The point repeatedly made by the governor is that the reserves are too low - currently at 1.09 months imports cover - and that they have to be built up to the commonly acceptable level of three months. In the last eight years such a target was approached fleetingly for a couple of months in 1992 at just over 2.8 months cover and that was after three years of deep recession and suppression of import demand. Given the structure of our balance of payments the target is but pie in the sky.

However, with the lines of credit taken into account an apparent cover of three months is achievable. Whether this will cut any ice with a sceptical market which is capable of understanding the makeup of the reserve position is another matter.

The governor's reference to a package of reconstruction measures also underlines that he was reading from a dated script. Such a package has been presented by government in the form of the Macroeconomic Strategy. But this package is for structural reform with its objectives to be realised at the end of the century. So the fullfillment of that condition, too, is remote.

However, some progress on both accounts could be made with the privatisation programme if that should involve a foreign participation entailing a substantial inflow of capital. But the plans of privatisation would appear to be cautious, politically sensitive, and possibly nationalistic, and certainly not with a mind to solving the exchange control problem.

The third point about the economic consequences of abolition is very real. A drain on financial resources would put considerable pressure on interest rates, which would be inimical to growth and harmful to the fiscal balance for borrowing rates would escalate. The happy assumption made by many commentators that foreign capital would flow in in sufficient quantity to offset the drain from domestic institutions investing abroad is breathtakingly naive.
The upshot of all this is that government must opt for gradualism.

However, I believe the authorities are misleading the country in dressing up the issue of abolition in terms of the defence of the rand and of the value of the currency. The debate is joined on the role of exchange controls in protecting the rand. Government talks of the set of measures, including exchange controls, needed to maintain the external viability of the rand. On the other hand the protagonists of the big bang make bold assertions that the rand will bounce back from an initial drop, will stabilise, and foreign capital will be attracted again.

Meanwhile the markets have demonstrated this year that the rand can be determined regardless of the existence of exchange controls and of structural reform packages. In short the integrity of the rand is irrelevant in justifying the retention of exchange controls.

I believe the truth of the matter is that exchange controls are required, and will continue to be so for a number of years, in order to retain loanable funds in this country for the purposes of development. The debate should be in these terms. The developmental requirements are massive and beyond dispute. The problem is the adequacy and mechanisms of funding. Any haemorrhaging of funds abroad, although undoubtedly in the interests of institutional portfolio diversification, would reduce the pool of loanable funds and put pressure on interest rates, with the undesirable economic consequences already mentioned.

It is not sufficient to suppose or hope that foreign investors would make adequate compensatory investment in South Africa. Even if of sufficient quantity, the investments in the main will be portfolio investments in stocks and shares and will be volatile. They will be highly liquid and not available for schemes of development where there is a loss of marketability and liquidity.
At its most cynical domestic loanable funds are captive whereas foreign funds are free and uncertain.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
